note: Built by tools/course_rework.py from Kyenzo's own games; every position checked by Stockfish 16.

types.name: Rook endings
steps: Put your rook behind the passed pawn: behind your own to push it, behind theirs to stop it.
An active rook is worth a pawn. Do not guard a pawn from the side if you can attack something instead.
Cut their king off along a file or a rank before you push.
Winning with a pawn on the 7th: build the bridge (Lucena). Defending: rook on your third rank, then checks from behind (Philidor).
Check from far away, from the long side: three files or more between your rook and the pawn.
Trade into the pawn ending only after you counted that it wins.

lessons.title: Lucena and Philidor (level 2)
lessons.takeaway: Rooks belong behind passed pawns; Lucena builds the bridge, Philidor waits on the third rank and then checks from behind.
rules: Two positions decide a huge share of rook endings: Lucena wins by building a bridge, Philidor draws with the third-rank defence.
Rooks belong behind Passer Winconditions — behind your own (the rook pushes) and behind the enemy's (the rook attacks while the enemy rook stays stuck in front). Tarrasch's rule.
Activity first. An active rook is often worth a pawn. A rook passively guarding a pawn is a bad investment.
Cut off the enemy king. A king cut off from the Passer Wincondition by your rook is out of the game — the first step of almost every winning rook ending.

Lucena position — WIN ("building a bridge"). Pawn on the 7th (not a rook pawn), attacking king on the promotion square, defending king cut off from the pawn. Method: check the defending king one file further away, lift your rook to the 4th rank, walk your king out, and block the last check with the rook.

Philidor position — DRAW ("third-rank defence"). Defending king on the promotion square; defending rook on its own third rank, keeping the attacking king off the 6th. The moment the pawn advances to the 6th, swing the rook to the far end of the board and check from behind: the king has lost its shelter.
Two connected Passer Winconditions on the 6th rank usually beat a lone rook when both kings are far away — unless the rook can win one of them at once, with tempo.
Cut-off geometry — ranks and files are walls built by rooks.

lessons.title: The practical rook ending (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Down a pawn, activate before you defend; check from a distance of at least three files.
rules: Rook endings are the most common and the most drawish: activity first, short side and long side, and exact checking distance.
The rook on the 7th rank attacks pawns from the side and cages the enemy king on the back rank.
Down a pawn? Activate before you defend. Give a second pawn if needed to activate rook and king. Passive defence usually loses slowly.
Short side, long side. The defending king goes to the short side of the pawn (fewer files); the defending rook goes to the long side to check from the flank.

Checking distance. Flank checks normally need three empty files between the checking rook and the pawn (sometimes two with the pawn on the 7th). Any closer, and the attacking king simply walks up to the rook.

Passive back-rank defence holds only against knight and rook pawns. Refines R1.20. Against bishop and centre pawns it loses once the attacking king reaches the 6th rank on the short side of its pawn: the pawn shields the king from flank checks and the back rank collapses. Use Philidor's defence while you still can.
3 vs 2 and 4 vs 3 on the same wing are usually drawn in rook endings. An extra pawn wins far more often when it is a distant Passer Wincondition.
"All rook endings are drawn." Tartakower's quip is a warning, not a law. Rook endings are the most common endgame type and among the most drawish: a pawn up is not yet a win.

lessons.title: The rook canon: Rule of Five, Vančura and the g7/h7 rule (level 4)
lessons.takeaway: Rook behind the pawn, flank checks from distance, and the defending king on g7 or h7 against a rook pawn.
rules: The great rook-ending positions are anchors: know exactly when they draw and when they lose.

R3A.5 (Principle). The Rule of Five. Pawn protected, defending king cut off by files: add the pawn's rank to the number of files the defending king is cut off. More than five: usually a win. Five or less: normally a draw. Knight and rook pawns are exceptions.
R3A.6 (Theory). Against a pawn on the 7th, only flank checks work; against a pawn on the 6th, checks from behind work too — the Philidor mechanism.

R3A.7 (Theory). Vančura position — DRAW. Rook pawn on the 6th with the attacking rook in front of it: the defending rook attacks the pawn from the side along the 6th rank, and the defending king shuttles between g7 and h7 (against an a-pawn). Meet the approaching king with checks from the side, keeping your distance; if the pawn advances to the 7th, put the rook behind it (R3A.8).

R3A.8 (Theory). The g7/h7 rule. Rook pawn on the 7th, attacking rook in front (Ra8, Pa7), defending rook behind the pawn: a draw with the defending king on g7 or h7. Anywhere else, a rook check or skewer usually forces the pawn through (e.g., Rh8! Rxa7, Rh7+).

R3A.9 (Principle). Rook + two pawns vs rook usually wins — connected pawns most easily. The notorious exception is f- and h-pawns: often a theoretical draw with an excellent defence, yet regularly lost in practice.

R3A.10 (Principle). Rook vs connected Passer Winconditions. Refines R1.21. The rook attacks from behind and the rook side's king must come fast; the pawns win when they reach the 6th with tempo and the rook cannot pick one of them off.
P3A.1 (Must-know position). Vančura. FEN: R7/6k1/P4r2/8/2K5/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.

lessons.title: The grandmaster layer of rook endings (level 5)
lessons.takeaway: Know the drawing zones exactly, so you can calculate transitions into R+P versus R long before they happen.
rules: Activity can outweigh two pawns: the side that completes its triangle of active rook, active king and passer first usually wins.

R3B.20 (Principle). Tarrasch's rule serves activity, not the other way round. Refines R1.16. If a rook in front of or beside a passed pawn is more active — cutting off the king, attacking pawns — activity wins the argument.
R3B.21 (Principle). In rook endings, counterplay beats passive material defence. The side that creates a Passer Wincondition first often wins even while behind in pawns.
R3C.12 (Principle). Activity can outweigh two pawns. When your rook is the most active piece on the board and your king escorts a Passer Wincondition, material counts less than tempo.

R3C.13 (Principle). The activity triangle (teaching model): active rook + active king + Passer Wincondition. The side that completes its triangle first usually wins; defend by breaking one side of the opponent's triangle.

R3C.14 (Theory). Know the drawing zones exactly — Philidor, Vančura, flank checks with enough distance, the Rule of Five, the g7/h7 rule — so you can calculate transitions into R+P vs R long before they happen.

theory.title: Lucena: build the bridge
how: Your pawn is on the 7th, your king on the queening square, their king cut off. This wins.
1. Check their king one file further away (Rd1+).
2. Lift your rook to the 4th rank (Rd4).
3. Walk your king out towards the rook's side; when the checks come, block with the rook on the 4th: the bridge.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: +5.2 for the side to move

theory.title: Philidor: the third-rank defence
how: Black to move. Keep your rook on the 6th rank (your third rank): their king cannot come forward.
When the pawn steps to the 6th, your rook goes to the 1st rank and checks from behind: their king has no shelter any more.
Keep your king in front of the pawn.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: +0.0 for the side to move

theory.title: Rook against pawn: cut the king off
how: Rook against a pawn with their king next to it: cut their king off from the pawn first.
Here Ra5! cuts it along the 5th rank; then the rook and your king win the pawn.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: +5.0 for the side to move

types.name: King and pawn endings
steps: Count first: every tempo decides. Whose king reaches the key squares first?
The opposition: kings facing each other with one square between; the side NOT to move holds it.
Key squares: with your king on a key square of your pawn, the pawn queens whoever moves.
The rule of the square: draw the square from the pawn to the last rank. A king inside it catches the pawn.
An outside passed pawn wins: it pulls their king away, your king eats the other side.
Defending: keep your king in front of the pawn. A rook pawn with your king in the corner is a draw.

lessons.title: The rule of the square and your first passed pawns (level 1)
lessons.takeaway: Draw the square before you move: inside it the king catches the pawn, outside it the pawn runs.
rules: A defending king that stands inside the pawn's square, or steps into it, catches the pawn. Rook pawns, the corner and the king in front of the pawn complete the foundation.

Rule of the square — stopping a Passer Wincondition with the king. Draw a square from the pawn to its promotion rank. If the defending king is inside it, or steps into it with the move, it catches the pawn (provided nothing blocks its path). A pawn on its starting square counts from one square further, because of the double step.
King in front, pawn behind. In K+P vs K, lead with the king; the pawn follows.
The rook pawn is special. K + rook pawn vs K is a draw once the defending king reaches the corner in front of the pawn.
Push your Passer Wincondition when it is safe. Every step forward ties down more enemy force.
Blockade enemy Passer Winconditions on the square directly in front of them.

Passer Wincondition vocabulary. Passed pawn · protected passer (defended by a pawn) · connected passers (adjacent files) · outside passer (far from the other pawns) · candidate (a pawn that can become a passer).
The square. FEN: 7k/8/8/8/1p3K2/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.

lessons.title: Opposition and key squares (level 2)
lessons.takeaway: Ask where your king must stand, not which pawn move to play.
rules: Opposition is the tool, key squares are the goal: it decides every king-and-pawn ending.

Opposition. Kings on the same file, rank or diagonal with one square between them: the side not to move has the opposition. With three or five squares between them it is distant opposition — same logic.
Key squares decide K+P vs K. If the attacking king reaches a key square and the pawn cannot be captured, it wins — no matter who is to move.
– Pawn on its 2nd–4th rank: the three squares two ranks in front of it.
– Pawn on its 5th–6th rank: the three squares one rank in front and the three squares two ranks in front.
– Rook pawn: only the two squares on the adjacent file that touch the promotion square (White a-pawn: b7 and b8).
Shortcut. With your pawn on the 4th or 5th rank (not a rook pawn), a king on the 6th rank — on the pawn's file or an adjacent file — always stands on a key square.
Opposition is the tool; key squares are the goal. Use the opposition to shoulder your way onto a key square.

lessons.title: Outside, protected and separated passed pawns (level 2)
lessons.takeaway: Use the outside passer as a decoy, then count the race to the last tempo.
rules: A passed pawn is a Passer Wincondition: used as a decoy it drags the enemy king away, and in a race the details decide.
The outside Passer Wincondition wins pawn endings. Use it as a decoy: while the enemy king runs to stop it, your king invades on the other wing.
A protected Passer Wincondition cannot be captured by the king alone. As long as its protector stands, the enemy king stays tied to it.
Separated Passer Winconditions overload a lone king. Check each one with the rule of the square — often one of them promotes.

Passer Wincondition races. Count the moves to promotion for both sides. Then check the details: does a queen arrive with check, and can the first queen stop the second (by controlling its promotion square, or by skewering king and new queen)?
Decoy — an outside Passer Wincondition pulls the enemy king away from the real battlefield.
Underpromotion — a knight for a check or fork, a rook to avoid stalemate (P2.3).
The outside Passer Wincondition as decoy. FEN: 8/8/3k4/8/P2K2p1/6P1/8/8 w - - 0 1.

lessons.title: Triangulation, shouldering and the Réti manoeuvre (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Count tempi and routes: the diagonal is as short as the straight line.
rules: Tempo is the currency of pawn endings: triangulate to hand over the move, shoulder the enemy king away and use diagonal king walks.
Triangulation. If the position is won with the opponent to move, and your king can use three squares while the enemy king has only two useful ones, walk the triangle to lose a tempo.
A knight cannot lose a tempo. It changes square colour on every move, so it can never return to the same square in an odd number of moves. Kings, bishops, rooks and queens can.
Distant and diagonal opposition follow the same parity logic — take them early to win the race to the key squares.
Shouldering. Use your king's body to block the enemy king's route. Often stronger than approaching directly.
The Réti manoeuvre. A king moving diagonally can chase two goals at once — hunting an enemy Passer Wincondition while supporting its own. Count diagonal routes before you give up a race.
Tempo economy — pawn endings are arithmetic: moves to promote, spare moves, king steps.
Two-goal geometry — the diagonal is as short as the straight line (Réti).

lessons.title: Breakthroughs, majorities, tempi and rook pawns (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: The candidate moves first; count spare tempi before the kings reach zugzwang.
rules: Three pawns against three can create a passer by force; majorities, reserve tempi and the rook pawn decide the rest.
The breakthrough. Three pawns on the 5th facing three on the 7th, kings far away: a pawn sacrifice creates a Passer Wincondition by force.
The candidate moves first. In a pawn majority, advance the pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it — your future Passer Wincondition. The others support it.
Healthy majorities create Passer Winconditions; crippled (doubled) majorities often cannot.
Reserve tempi decide blocked pawn endings. Count spare pawn moves on both sides before the kings reach zugzwang. Doubled pawns can be a hidden source of tempi.
The more active king usually decides the pawn ending.
Rook pawns are the most drawish pawns in pawn, bishop and rook endings, and against a queen on the 7th. Against a knight they are the most dangerous.
The breakthrough. FEN: 6k1/ppp5/8/PPP5/8/8/8/6K1 w - - 0 1.

lessons.title: Corresponding squares and mined squares (level 4)
lessons.takeaway: Find the key squares first, then map the correspondence backwards.
rules: Opposition is the simplest case of corresponding squares; some squares are mines where the side that steps on them loses.

R3A.1 (Theory). Corresponding squares. Opposition is a special case of a larger system: every square of the attacking king has a matching square for the defending king. Find the key squares first, then map the correspondence backwards.
R3A.2 (Theory). Mined squares (mutual zugzwang). Some squares are mines — whoever steps on them first loses. Approach them only with the move in hand.

theory.title: Key squares: the king in front wins
how: Your king on e4 stands on a key square of the e2-pawn (d4, e4 and f4).
From a key square the pawn queens, whoever is to move: keep the king in front and push the pawn only when the king has room.
Use the opposition to keep their king out: when the kings face each other, make them step aside.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: +35.8 for the side to move

theory.title: Opposition: the defender holds
how: Black to move. Take the opposition: Kf7, facing the white king with one square between.
Keep facing their king. If you step aside, their king reaches a key square and the pawn queens.
When the pawn reaches the 7th rank with check, step straight in front of it (to the queening square): then it is stalemate or the pawn falls.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: -0.0 for the side to move

theory.title: The rule of the square
how: Draw the square from the b4-pawn to b1: b4, e4, e1, b1.
Your king on f4 can step into it with Ke3: inside the square it catches the pawn.
Then take the pawn: king against king is a draw.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: +0.0 for the side to move

theory.title: Rook pawn: the corner draws
how: Black to move. With a rook pawn, your king in the corner (h8) is a draw.
Stay on h8 and g8. Their king cannot drive you out without stalemate.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: -0.0 for the side to move

types.name: Queen endings
steps: Centralise the queen first: the centre gives checks on every side.
The king hides close to the enemy king or in front of its own passed pawn.
Your passed pawn is the plan: every check you can stop with a block that pushes it is a gain.
Queen against a pawn on the 7th: check and pin until their king stands in front of its pawn, then bring your king one step.
Defending: perpetual check is your draw. Look for it before every move.

lessons.title: Queen versus a pawn on the seventh (level 2)
lessons.takeaway: Check and pin until the king steps in front of its pawn, and never capture into a stalemate.
rules: A queen usually stops a pawn on the seventh, but against bishop and rook pawns the stalemate tricks save the defender.

Queen vs pawn on the 7th, defending king beside it. The queen wins against centre (d/e) and knight (b/g) pawns. Against bishop (c/f) and rook (a/h) pawns it is a draw by stalemate tricks — unless the attacking king is already close.
Queen vs pawn — the method. Check and pin until the defending king must step in front of its pawn. That buys one tempo for your king to approach. Repeat.

lessons.title: Queen endings: winning zone, fortresses and cross-checks (level 4)
lessons.takeaway: Use cross-checks against perpetual, and never capture the pawn when it is stalemate.
rules: The queen beats most pawns and the rook, but stalemate tricks, fortresses and perpetual check are the defender's resources.

R3A.11 (Theory). The winning zone. Refines R1.13. Against bishop and rook pawns on the 7th, the queen still wins when the attacking king is close enough to create a Mate Wincondition or to support the capture.

R3A.12 (Theory). Queen vs rook is a win (barring immediate tactics). Drive the king to the edge, then separate rook and king by zugzwang — the queen can pass the move with a triangle of checks (P3A.4) — and finish with a fork or mate.
R3A.13 (Theory). Queen vs rook + pawn can be a fortress. A rook on its third rank, protected by a pawn on its second rank next to its king, often cannot be broken.
R3A.14 (Principle). In queen endings the Passer Wincondition outranks material. A far-advanced passer escorted by the queen beats one or two extra pawns elsewhere.

R3A.15 (Principle). Perpetual check is the defender's main denial tool. The attacker centralises the queen, uses pawns as shelter, and answers checks with cross-checks — blocking a check while giving check.
C3A.5 (Concept). Cross-check — blocking a check with a check; the attacker's weapon against perpetual.
P3A.2 (Must-know position). Queen vs bishop pawn. FEN: 7K/8/6Q1/8/8/8/1kp5/8 w - - 0 1.

lessons.title: Queen and heavy-piece endings at master level (level 5)
lessons.takeaway: King safety, colour complexes and passers decide, not slogans.
rules: Queen endings are races of passers and checks; trust the position rather than the piece myth.
R3B.25 (Principle). Queen vs two rooks. Rooks are strong when they protect each other; the queen wins with forks against loose rooks and with attacks on weak pawns and the king.

R3C.15 (Principle). Queen endings are races of Passer Winconditions and checks. The attacking king walks toward its passed pawn or toward the enemy king, where checks can be blocked with cross-checks.

R3C.16 (Principle). Trust the position, not the piece myth. Capablanca's claims that queen + knight beats queen + bishop, and rook + bishop beats rook + knight, hold only by small statistical margins (Kaufman). King safety, colour complexes and Passer Winconditions decide.

theory.title: Queen against a pawn on the 7th
how: Check and pin until their king has to stand in front of its own pawn.
That gives you a free move: bring your king one step closer. Repeat until your king helps to win the pawn or mate.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: +35.2 for the side to move

types.name: Knight against bishop
types.what: One knight against one bishop, plus pawns.
steps: The bishop wants open play and pawns on both wings; the knight wants a closed position and pawns on one wing.
Put your pawns on the colour your bishop does NOT control, so the bishop defends them from far and the king blocks the rest.
A knight needs a protected square (an outpost) that no pawn can attack.
The king goes to the side where the play is, usually to attack the pawns on the bishop's other colour.
A knight cannot lose a tempo: in tight positions that decides.

lessons.title: Good bishop, bad bishop, bishop versus knight and the blockade (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop and blockade with a knight or the king.
rules: Pawns on the bishop's colour make it bad; knights love closed positions and blockade squares; knight endings behave like pawn endings.

Good bishop, bad bishop. A bishop is bad when its own pawns are fixed on its colour. Put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop; fix enemy pawns on the colour of your bishop so you can attack them.
Bishop vs knight. Bishops prefer open positions and pawns on both wings; knights prefer closed positions, outposts and all pawns on one wing.
Knight endings behave like pawn endings (Botvinnik). The outside Passer Wincondition and king activity are even more decisive than usual.
Blockade with the right piece. The knight is the ideal blockader of a Passer Wincondition — it stays active on the blockade square. In endings, so is the king.
Colour complexes — a bishop fights for one colour; pawns and the king must cover the other.
Blockade — the main Wincondition-denial tool in minor-piece endings.

lessons.title: Knight, bishop and pawn endings (level 4)
lessons.takeaway: Control the promotion square or reach it in time; K+N versus K is a dead position.
rules: Rook pawns are the knight's nightmare, bishops need a diagonal across the pawn's path, and a knight can give itself up for the last pawn.
R3A.20 (Principle). Knight vs rook pawn on the 7th. The knight holds only if it controls the promotion square or reaches it in time. Rook pawns are the knight's nightmare.

R3A.24 (Principle). Bishop + pawn vs same-coloured bishop. A draw if the defending king gets in front of the pawn on a square the attacking bishop cannot attack. Otherwise the result depends on whether the defending bishop keeps a diagonal across the pawn's path that the attacker cannot cut.

R3A.25 (Principle). Knight + pawn vs knight is usually a draw with the defending king in front — and the defending knight can often give itself up for the last pawn, since K+N vs K is a dead position.

lessons.title: Knight versus bad bishop and bishop versus knight (level 5)
lessons.takeaway: Fix pawns on the bishop's colour, occupy key squares and use zugzwang.
rules: A knight against a bad bishop generates Winconditions by itself; with pawns on both wings, create a passer on one wing and invade on the other.
R3B.22 (Principle). Knight vs bad bishop is a Wincondition generator. Fix pawns on the bishop's colour, occupy the key squares with the king, and use zugzwang.
R3B.23 (Principle). Bishop vs knight with pawns on both wings. Create a Passer Wincondition on one wing to deflect the knight, then invade on the other.

types.name: Opposite-coloured bishops
types.what: One bishop each, on different colours.
steps: The defender builds a fortress: the king blocks one passed pawn, the bishop stops the other from far.
The attacker needs two passed pawns far apart (best: three files or more), one for the king and one for the bishop.
Pawns on the colour of the defending bishop are targets; put yours on your own bishop's colour when you defend.
Two pawns up is often still a draw. Count the files between the passed pawns before you trade.

lessons.title: Opposite-coloured bishops (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Bishops only: blockade on your bishop's colour. With heavy pieces: attack the colour their bishop cannot guard.
rules: Alone, opposite-coloured bishops are drawish even a pawn or two down; with rooks or queens they favour the attacker.
Opposite-coloured bishops, bishops only: an extra pawn is usually a draw — often two extra pawns as well. The defender places his pawns on his bishop's colour and blockades on that colour.
Opposite-coloured bishops with rooks or queens favour the attacking side. The defending bishop cannot help on the other colour complex, so the Mate Wincondition grows stronger.

lessons.title: Opposite-coloured bishops: the winning recipe (level 5)
lessons.takeaway: One file apart is usually a draw; three or more files normally wins.
rules: To win with opposite-coloured bishops you need two passers far apart; connected passers must reach the sixth rank.

R3B.24 (Principle). Opposite-coloured bishops — the winning recipe. Refines R2.22. You need two Passer Winconditions far apart. With one file between them it is usually a draw; the wider the gap the better, and three or more files apart normally wins. Connected passers need to reach the 6th rank. Beware the wrong rook pawn.

types.name: Same-coloured bishops
types.what: One bishop each, on the same colour.
steps: A good bishop sees the squares its own pawns do not stand on; a bad bishop is locked by its pawns.
Fix their pawns on your bishop's colour, then attack them.
Your king decides: bring it to the side where their pawns are weak.
With bishop + rook pawn: if the bishop does not control the queening corner and their king gets there, it is a draw.

lessons.title: The wrong bishop and minor pieces against passed pawns (level 2)
lessons.takeaway: If the bishop does not control the corner, the corner is a fortress.
rules: A bishop with a rook pawn only wins if it controls the promotion square, and minor pieces stop passers in different ways.

The wrong bishop. Bishop + rook pawn vs king is a draw when the bishop does not control the promotion square and the defending king reaches the corner. Extra pawns on the same rook file change nothing.
Bishops stop Passer Winconditions from a distance; knights stop them best from directly in front — and knights struggle against rook pawns.
The wrong bishop. FEN: k7/8/PK6/8/8/4B3/8/8 b - - 0 1.
Draw: the dark-squared bishop can never control a8.

lessons.title: Good bishop, bad bishop, bishop versus knight and the blockade (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop and blockade with a knight or the king.
rules: Pawns on the bishop's colour make it bad; knights love closed positions and blockade squares; knight endings behave like pawn endings.

Good bishop, bad bishop. A bishop is bad when its own pawns are fixed on its colour. Put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop; fix enemy pawns on the colour of your bishop so you can attack them.
Bishop vs knight. Bishops prefer open positions and pawns on both wings; knights prefer closed positions, outposts and all pawns on one wing.
Knight endings behave like pawn endings (Botvinnik). The outside Passer Wincondition and king activity are even more decisive than usual.
Blockade with the right piece. The knight is the ideal blockader of a Passer Wincondition — it stays active on the blockade square. In endings, so is the king.
Colour complexes — a bishop fights for one colour; pawns and the king must cover the other.
Blockade — the main Wincondition-denial tool in minor-piece endings.

theory.title: The wrong bishop
how: Black to move. Their bishop is light-squared, the queening square h8 is dark: the wrong bishop.
Go to the corner and stay there (h8, g8, h7). Nothing can drive your king out without stalemate.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: -0.0 for the side to move

types.name: Knight endings
steps: Knight endings play like pawn endings: the king and the passed pawn decide.
An outside passed pawn is even stronger with knights: a knight is slow to come back.
Look for the knight check that forks king and pawn, and the fork that trades into a won pawn ending.
A knight stops a pawn best from in front of it.

lessons.title: Knight, bishop and pawn endings (level 4)
lessons.takeaway: Control the promotion square or reach it in time; K+N versus K is a dead position.
rules: Rook pawns are the knight's nightmare, bishops need a diagonal across the pawn's path, and a knight can give itself up for the last pawn.
R3A.20 (Principle). Knight vs rook pawn on the 7th. The knight holds only if it controls the promotion square or reaches it in time. Rook pawns are the knight's nightmare.

R3A.24 (Principle). Bishop + pawn vs same-coloured bishop. A draw if the defending king gets in front of the pawn on a square the attacking bishop cannot attack. Otherwise the result depends on whether the defending bishop keeps a diagonal across the pawn's path that the attacker cannot cut.

R3A.25 (Principle). Knight + pawn vs knight is usually a draw with the defending king in front — and the defending knight can often give itself up for the last pawn, since K+N vs K is a dead position.

types.name: Rook against a minor piece
types.what: A rook against a knight or a bishop.
steps: Up the exchange: keep pawns on both wings, open files for the rook, and trade pawns only when your king can win the rest.
Rook against bishop without pawns: the defender's king goes to the corner the bishop does not control.
Rook against knight without pawns: keep the knight next to its king; a knight cut off from its king can be lost.
The defender wants pawns on one wing and a fortress for the minor piece.

lessons.title: Rook versus a minor piece: the corner decides (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Against a bishop run to the corner not of its colour; against a knight stay next to your knight and avoid corners.
rules: Without pawns a rook usually cannot beat a minor piece: the defender has to run to the right corner.

Rook vs minor piece without pawns is generally a draw. With a bishop, the defending king runs to the corner not of the bishop's colour — there the bishop can block checks. With a knight, keep the knight next to your king and avoid corners.
Rook vs bishop: the corner decides.
7k/8/6K1/3b4/8/8/8/R7 w - - 0 1 — Draw: the king sits in the corner not of its bishop's colour, so a check on the 8th rank is blocked on g8.
k7/8/1K6/3b4/8/8/8/7R w - - 0 1 — White wins: 1.Rh8+ Bg8 2.Rxg8 mate. Same material, wrong corner.

lessons.title: Pawnless endings: 2B v N, R+B v R, queen v minor pieces (level 4)
lessons.takeaway: Know the winning and drawing verdicts, and count the 50 moves yourself.
rules: Tablebases overturned old verdicts: two bishops beat a knight, queen beats two bishops, but the 50-move rule can rescue the defender.
R3A.19 (Theory). Two bishops vs knight (no pawns) is generally a win — tablebases overturned the old drawing verdict — but some wins exceed the 50-move limit.

R3A.21 (Theory). Rook + bishop vs rook is generally a theoretical draw — but hard to defend. Winning positions: Philidor's and Lolli's. Drawing methods: the Cochrane defence (pin the bishop to its king, away from the edge) and the second-rank defence.
R3A.22 (Theory). Rook + knight vs rook is a draw and much easier to hold.

R3A.23 (Theory). Queen vs two bishops: the queen wins most positions , but it can take up to 71 moves — the 50-move rule can rescue the defender. Queen vs two knights: the queen wins many positions, but the knights hold a large share of draws.

lessons.title: Material by the numbers and up the exchange (level 5)
lessons.takeaway: Up the exchange: keep pawns on both wings and avoid fortress structures.
rules: Database numbers: bishop and knight are equal on average, the bishop pair is worth about half a pawn, rooks gain value as pawns disappear.

R3B.9 (Principle). Material by the numbers (Kaufman's database findings). An unpaired bishop and a knight are equal on average — the position decides. The bishop pair is worth about half a pawn. With six or more pawns each the knight is marginally better, with four or fewer the bishop; rooks gain value as pawns disappear.

R3B.10 (Principle). Up the exchange? Keep pawns on both wings and avoid structures where the minor piece and pawns can build a fortress. Returning the exchange at the right moment is often the cleanest win.

theory.title: Rook against bishop: the right corner
how: Black to move. Rook against bishop with no pawns is a draw when your king uses the corner the bishop does NOT control.
Your bishop is light-squared and h8 is dark: stay near h8 and keep the bishop next to the king, out of forks.
Survive 50 moves without a capture and it is a draw (the 50-move rule), or repeat the position.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: -0.3 for the side to move

types.name: Rook and minor piece each
types.what: Rook + knight or bishop on both sides.
steps: Find the worst piece on each side; improving yours is the plan.
Decide which trade helps you: trade the rooks or the minor pieces, but only into an ending you counted.
Rook + bishop work well with pawns on both wings; rook + knight with play on one side.
King activity still counts: bring it to the centre once the queens are off.

lessons.title: Two weaknesses, do not hurry and the pawn-ending test (Tier 2 checklist) (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Create a second weakness, do not hurry, and run the pawn-ending test before every trade.
rules: One weakness can be defended, two cannot. When the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first.
The principle of two weaknesses. One weakness can be defended. Create a second one on the other wing and switch between them until the defence breaks.
Do not hurry. If the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first. The decisive break comes when everything is ready.
The pawn-ending test. Before trading into a pawn ending, remove all pieces in your head and ask who wins. Winning → trade. Not winning → keep pieces.
Weakness targeting — fix the pawn, attack it with more pieces than can defend it, then add a second target.
Typical errors at Tier 2:
– Entering a rook ending a pawn up and treating it as won (R2.18).
– Waiting passively on the back rank against a centre pawn (R2.16).

lessons.takeaway: Up the exchange: keep pawns on both wings and avoid fortress structures.
rules: Database numbers: bishop and knight are equal on average, the bishop pair is worth about half a pawn, rooks gain value as pawns disappear.

R3B.9 (Principle). Material by the numbers (Kaufman's database findings). An unpaired bishop and a knight are equal on average — the position decides. The bishop pair is worth about half a pawn. With six or more pawns each the knight is marginally better, with four or fewer the bishop; rooks gain value as pawns disappear.

R3B.10 (Principle). Up the exchange? Keep pawns on both wings and avoid structures where the minor piece and pawns can build a fortress. Returning the exchange at the right moment is often the cleanest win.

types.name: Two rooks each
steps: Double rooks on an open file, then go to the 7th rank: two rooks on the 7th often mate or win pawns.
Trade one pair of rooks when you are ahead: one rook each is simpler to win.
When you are worse, keep both rooks: more pieces, more chances for checks and counterplay.

lessons.title: The practical rook ending (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Down a pawn, activate before you defend; check from a distance of at least three files.
rules: Rook endings are the most common and the most drawish: activity first, short side and long side, and exact checking distance.
The rook on the 7th rank attacks pawns from the side and cages the enemy king on the back rank.
Down a pawn? Activate before you defend. Give a second pawn if needed to activate rook and king. Passive defence usually loses slowly.
Short side, long side. The defending king goes to the short side of the pawn (fewer files); the defending rook goes to the long side to check from the flank.

Checking distance. Flank checks normally need three empty files between the checking rook and the pawn (sometimes two with the pawn on the 7th). Any closer, and the attacking king simply walks up to the rook.

Passive back-rank defence holds only against knight and rook pawns. Refines R1.20. Against bishop and centre pawns it loses once the attacking king reaches the 6th rank on the short side of its pawn: the pawn shields the king from flank checks and the back rank collapses. Use Philidor's defence while you still can.
3 vs 2 and 4 vs 3 on the same wing are usually drawn in rook endings. An extra pawn wins far more often when it is a distant Passer Wincondition.
"All rook endings are drawn." Tartakower's quip is a warning, not a law. Rook endings are the most common endgame type and among the most drawish: a pawn up is not yet a win.

types.name: Piece against pawns
types.what: One side has a minor piece, the other only pawns.
steps: Count: can the piece stop the pawns, or do two connected pawns on the 6th beat it?
The king must help: the side whose king reaches the pawns first decides.
A knight against a rook pawn on the 7th is the hardest case for the knight; a bishop stops pawns from far.

lessons.title: The wrong bishop and minor pieces against passed pawns (level 2)
lessons.takeaway: If the bishop does not control the corner, the corner is a fortress.
rules: A bishop with a rook pawn only wins if it controls the promotion square, and minor pieces stop passers in different ways.

The wrong bishop. Bishop + rook pawn vs king is a draw when the bishop does not control the promotion square and the defending king reaches the corner. Extra pawns on the same rook file change nothing.
Bishops stop Passer Winconditions from a distance; knights stop them best from directly in front — and knights struggle against rook pawns.
The wrong bishop. FEN: k7/8/PK6/8/8/4B3/8/8 b - - 0 1.
Draw: the dark-squared bishop can never control a8.

lessons.title: Rook versus a minor piece: the corner decides (level 3)
lessons.takeaway: Against a bishop run to the corner not of its colour; against a knight stay next to your knight and avoid corners.
rules: Without pawns a rook usually cannot beat a minor piece: the defender has to run to the right corner.

Rook vs minor piece without pawns is generally a draw. With a bishop, the defending king runs to the corner not of the bishop's colour — there the bishop can block checks. With a knight, keep the knight next to your king and avoid corners.
Rook vs bishop: the corner decides.
7k/8/6K1/3b4/8/8/8/R7 w - - 0 1 — Draw: the king sits in the corner not of its bishop's colour, so a check on the 8th rank is blocked on g8.
k7/8/1K6/3b4/8/8/8/7R w - - 0 1 — White wins: 1.Rh8+ Bg8 2.Rxg8 mate. Same material, wrong corner.

types.name: Basic mates
types.what: Mate with queen, rook, or bishop and knight.
steps: Queen or rook: build a box around their king and make it smaller with every move.
Bring your king close: the mate needs it (except the queen in the corner).
Stalemate check before every queen move: leave their king a free square until the mating move.
Bishop + knight: drive the king to the corner of the bishop's colour. The W-manoeuvre of the knight keeps it there.

lessons.title: Basic mates: queen, rook and the ladder (level 1)
lessons.takeaway: Shrink the box, bring your king, check last, and always ask whether the lone king still has a legal move.
rules: The lone king is always mated on the edge. Learn to shrink the box without giving stalemate.
In the basic mates (K+Q, K+R, K+2B, K+B+N vs K) the lone king is always mated on the edge. Drive it there.
The edge is a prison. Mate Wincondition technique means shrinking the enemy king's space (the "box") until it stands on the edge.
The basic mates — your first Mate Wincondition drills.
– K+Q vs K — shrink the box with the queen a knight's move away from the enemy king; when it reaches the edge, stop and bring your own king; mate with king support. At most 10 moves with best play.
– K+R vs K — the rook cuts the board, the king approaches; when the kings face each other, check from the side to push the enemy king back; use rook waiting moves. At most 16 moves.
– K+2R (or K+Q+R) vs K — the ladder: the heavy pieces alternate checks rank by rank. If the king attacks one of them, move it to the far end of its rank.
The stalemate trap. FEN: k7/8/1Q6/8/8/8/8/2K5 b - - 0 1.

lessons.title: Advanced mates and the Troitzky line (level 4)
lessons.takeaway: B+N: drive the king to the corner of the bishop's colour; 2N cannot mate, but 2N beat a pawn on or behind the Troitzky line.
rules: Bishop and knight, two bishops and two knights against a pawn are theoretical results you must be able to execute.
R3A.16 (Theory). K+B+N vs K is a forced mate in at most 33 moves: drive the king to a corner of the bishop's colour. Learn the knight's W-manoeuvre (or Delétang's triangle method).
R3A.17 (Theory). K+2B vs K is mate in at most 19 moves. Side-by-side bishops build a wall, the king approaches, and mate can be given in any corner.

R3A.18 (Theory). K+2N vs K cannot be forced — but K+2N vs K+P often can. The knights generally win when the pawn is securely blockaded by a knight on or behind the Troitzky line — Black pawns: a4, b6, c5, d4, e4, f5, g6, h4 (White pawns, mirrored: a5, b3, c4, d5, e5, f4, g3, h5). Some of these wins take more than 50 moves.

theory.title: Mate with the queen
how: Box their king in: put the queen a knight's move away from it and follow it.
When it is on the edge, bring your king, and stop to check for stalemate before every queen move.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: mate for the side to move

theory.title: Mate with the rook
how: Cut their king off with the rook, then bring your king to face it (the opposition).
Check when the kings face each other: the king goes back one rank. Repeat until the edge.
When the rook is attacked, move it to the far side and keep the box.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: +4.9 for the side to move

theory.title: Mate with bishop and knight
how: The hardest basic mate: you have 50 moves.
Drive their king to the edge, then to the corner of your bishop's colour (a1 or h8 for this dark bishop).
From the wrong corner, push it along the edge with the W-manoeuvre of the knight.
theory.proof: Stockfish 16, depth 20: +2.8 for the side to move
